title: Sanctions against KPMG LLP and Nick Plumb
text:
IN THE MATTER OF
THE EXECUTIVE COUNSEL OF THE FINANCIAL REPORTING COUNCIL
-and-
(1) KPMG LLP

(2) NICK PLUMB

FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE
Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive
Counsel following an investigation relating to, and admissions made by, the
Respondents. It does not make findings against any persons other than the
Respondents and it would not be fair to treat any part of this document as
constituting or evidencing findings against any other persons or entities since they
are not parties to the proceedings.
1.
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for statutory
audit in the UK and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the “AEP”), revised in
June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the investigation, prosecution
and sanctioning of breaches of Relevant Requirements.
1.2. The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined terms
are also used within this document. Where defined terms are used, they appear in italics.
1.3. This Final Settlement Decision Notice also uses the following definitions:
1.3.1.
“FY21” means the financial year ended 28 August 2021, “FY21 financial
statements” means Carr’s Group plc’s (“Carr’s”) consolidated financial

2
OFFICIAL
statements for that period, and “FY21 Audit” means the Statutory Audit of the
FY21 financial statements.
1.3.2.
“Respondents” means:
1.3.2.1. KPMG LLP (“KPMG”) which was the Statutory Audit Firm for the FY21
Audit.
1.3.2.2. Mr Nick Plumb, who was the Statutory Auditor for the FY21 Audit and
who signed off the FY21 Audit report on behalf of KPMG on 7
December 2021.
1.4. In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement
discussions with the Respondents.
1.5. A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued by Executive Counsel on 31 January
2025 pursuant to Rule 103 of the AEP in relation to the conduct of the Respondents in
respect of the FY21 Audit. The Respondents provided written agreement to the
Proposed Settlement Decision Notice, pursuant to Rule 105 of the AEP, on 4 February
2025. The Convener subsequently appointed an Independent Reviewer, pursuant to
Rule 106 of the AEP, to consider the Proposed Settlement Decision Notice.
1.6. On 24 February 2025, the Independent Reviewer approved the issuance of this Final
Settlement Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.
1.7. In accordance with Rule 108 of the AEP this Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out:
1.7.1.
the breaches of Relevant Requirement(s), with reasons;
1.7.2.
the Sanctions imposed on the Respondents, with reasons;
1.7.3.
the amount payable by the Respondents in respect of Executive Counsel’s
Costs.
1.8. This Final Settlement Decision Notice is divided into the following sections:
1.8.1.
Section 1: Introduction
1.8.2.
Section 2: Executive Summary of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.3.
Section 3: Background;
1.8.4.
Section 4: Relevant Requirements to which the breaches relate;
1.8.5.
Section 5: Details of the breaches of Relevant Requirements;
1.8.6.
Section 6: Sanctions; and
1.8.7.
Section 7: Costs.

3
OFFICIAL
2.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
2.1. Carr’s Group plc is the parent company of a corporate group operating in the agriculture
and engineering sectors (“the Carr’s Group”). In FY21 it was listed on the main market
of the London Stock Exchange and was a “Public Interest Entity” (“PIE”) for the purposes
of, among other matters, the application of the FRC’s Revised Ethical Standard 2019
(“the 2019 Ethical Standard”).
2.2. The Statutory Audit Firm for the FY21 financial statements of Carr’s was KPMG. Mr
Plumb acted as the Statutory Auditor of Carr’s for the FY21 Audit and signed the FY21
Audit report on behalf of KPMG.
2.3. The FY21 financial statements were prepared as group financial statements and
incorporated the financial results of subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates of Carr’s.
These included an associate called Carrs Billington Agriculture (Operations) Limited
(“CBAO”).
2.4. In FY21, CBAO was audited by a separate Statutory Audit Firm to KPMG, referred to
herein as “Firm X”. For the purposes of ISA 600, CBAO was a “component” of the group
of entities whose financial information was incorporated into Carr’s FY21 financial
statements, and Firm X was the “component auditor” of CBAO.
2.5. Since the Respondents intended to use the work of Firm X (as component auditor) for
the purposes of the FY21 Audit, the Respondents’ obligations as the Statutory Audit
Firm and Statutory Auditor included obligations in relation to the independence of Firm
X. These included an obligation under paragraph 1.47 of the 2019 Ethical Standard “to
obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and be satisfied that” [Firm X] “is independent of
each entity relevant to the engagement in accordance with supporting ethical provision
2.4 of this Ethical Standard”.
2.6. Supporting ethical provision A2.4 provides:
“For each engagement, the firm and the engagement partner (in the case of the
engagement partner insofar as they are able to do so) shall ensure that the firm’s
independence is not compromised as a result of conditions or relationships that
would compromise the independence of a network firm (whether or not its work is
used in the conduct of the engagement) or an other firm whose work is used in the
conduct of the engagement, having regard to the ethical requirements in this
Ethical Standard that are relevant to the engagement.”
2.7. For the FY21 Audit, the “ethical requirements in this Ethical Standard that are relevant
to the engagement” included the following:

4
OFFICIAL
2.7.1.
2019 Ethical Standard paragraph 3.10, which requires a “Key audit partner”1
(“KAP”) of a PIE to cease their participation in the statutory audit no later than
five years from the date of their appointment;
2.7.2.
2019 Ethical Standard paragraph 5.71, which prohibits a Statutory Audit Firm
from providing, to a “significant affiliate2” of a listed entity, services to prepare
current or deferred tax calculations that are or may reasonably be expected to
be used by the relevant entity when preparing accounting entries; and
2.7.3.
2019 Ethical Standard paragraph 5.120(a), which prohibits a Statutory Audit
Firm from providing “accounting services3” to a “significant affiliate” of a listed
entity, including where such services involve the preparation of financial
statements that are then subject to audit.
2.8. As the Respondents accept, they relied on the work of Firm X notwithstanding these
three ethical requirements were not complied with in FY21.
2.8.1.
The Senior Statutory Auditor for CBAO’s Statutory Audit in FY21 was a partner
of Firm X (referred to herein as “Firm X Partner”) and FY21 was his sixth year
in that role. Accordingly, he was prohibited by 2019 Ethical Standard paragraph
3.10 from participating as a KAP in the FY21 Audit4.
2.8.2.
For the purposes of the FY21 Audit, the Respondents should have treated
CBAO as a “significant affiliate” of a listed entity (namely Carr’s). Firm X
provided to CBAO services of the type prohibited by paragraphs 5.71 and
5.120(a) of the 2019 Ethical Standard.
2.9. In these circumstances, the Respondents should not have signed the FY21 audit report
whilst placing reliance on the work of Firm X.

1 Defined in the FRC Glossary of Terms (Auditing and Ethics) (December 2019). The limb of the
definition which is relevant to this FSDN provides that a KAP includes: “In the case of a group audit…the
statutory auditor designated at the level of material subsidiaries”. It is agreed between Executive
Counsel and the Respondents that CBAO was at all relevant times a “material subsidiary” in this
respect.

2 Defined in the FRC Glossary of Terms (Auditing and Ethics) (December 2019) and addressed
further at paragraph 5.13 below.

3 Defined in the FRC Glossary of Terms (Auditing and Ethics) (December 2019).

4 The exemptions in paragraphs 3.14 and 3.15 of the 2019 Ethical Standard were not applicable to the
FY21 Audit.

5
OFFICIAL
2.10. Although in FY21 the Respondents engaged with Firm X in relation to the independence
and ethical requirements applicable to Firm X, the Respondents failed to take any, or
any proper, account of information that was given to them by Firm X regarding that firm’s
independence and compliance with ethical requirements. On the basis of that
information, it should have been apparent to the Respondents that:
2.10.1. Firm X had a “long term association” with the CBAO audit; and
2.10.2. Firm X was providing services to CBAO of the nature summarised in
paragraphs 2.7.2 and 2.7.3 above, which were prohibited under the 2019
Ethical Standard.
2.11. The Respondents missed a number of opportunities to establish the relevant facts and
the non-compliance with the 2019 Ethical Standard, as regards KAP rotation and the
services that Firm X was prohibited from providing to CBAO.
2.12. The Respondents accept that in these circumstances they have breached the following
Relevant Requirements:
2.12.1. KAP rotation in relation to the Firm X Partner: Paragraph 1.47 (in conjunction
with A2.4) of the 2019 Ethical Standard, ISA 600.11 and ISA 600.19(a);
2.12.2. Provision of accounting services by Firm X: Paragraph 1.47 (in conjunction with
A2.4) of the 2019 Ethical Standard, ISA 600.19(a) and ISA 600.42; and
2.12.3. Provision of tax services by Firm X: Paragraph 1.47 (in conjunction with A2.4)
of the 2019 Ethical Standard, ISA 600.19(a) and ISA 600.42.
2.13. This Final Settlement Decision Notice sets out the following Sanctions in respect of the
Respondents:
KPMG
2.13.1. a financial Sanction of £1.25 million, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating
factors, discounted for exceptional cooperation by 15% and further discounted
for admissions and early disposal by 35%. Post adjustment financial sanction:
£690,625;
2.13.2. a published statement, in the form of a severe reprimand;
2.13.3. a declaration that the FY21 Audit report did not satisfy the Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice; and
2.13.4. a non-financial Sanction in the following terms:

6
OFFICIAL
KPMG shall, in respect of UK PIE statutory audits involving component
auditors outside of KPMG’s network, review a representative sample of
such files, agreed with EC and its FRC Supervisor and report to its FRC
Supervisor within 6 months of this FSDN, on whether compliance with the
Independence requirements in the FRC’s Ethical Standard has been
achieved in those cases and, in cases of non-compliance, the action
subsequently taken where such matters were identified. The scope and
process of the review shall be agreed with EC and the firm’s Supervisor.
The firm’s Supervisor may extend the reporting period for an additional
year if the results of the review indicate that there have been failures to
comply with the Independence requirements in the FRC’s Ethical
Standard, or if the Supervisor has concerns about the review work carried
out.
Mr Plumb
2.13.5. a financial Sanction of £70,000, adjusted for aggravating and mitigating factors,
discounted for exceptional cooperation by 15% and further discounted for
admissions and early disposal by 35%. Post adjustment financial sanction:
£38,675;
2.13.6. a published statement, in the form of a severe reprimand; and
2.13.7. a declaration that the FY21 Audit report did not satisfy the Relevant
Requirements, as set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice.
2.14. The discounts given for cooperation and settlement reflect that the Respondents self-
reported the breaches of Relevant Requirements and dealt promptly with settlement.
2.15. Additionally, Executive Counsel requires that the Respondents pay her costs in full in
this matter, being £219,755. Such costs shall be paid no later than 28 days after the
date of this Final Settlement Decision Notice.

3.
BACKGROUND
Parties

7
OFFICIAL
3.1. In 2021, KPMG was the second largest audit firm in the UK, with audit fee income of
£646m and 133 audit principals. In that year KPMG audited 293 PIEs5. One of those
was Carr’s, which KPMG audited in the financial years ended 31 August 2019 (“FY19”),
29 August 2020 (“FY20”) and FY21.
3.2. Mr Plumb was at all material times a partner of KPMG. He is admitted as a member of
the Institute of Chartered Accountants of England and Wales. He was the Senior Statutory
Auditor for KPMG’s Statutory Audit of Carr’s for each of FY19, FY20 and FY21. He
signed, on KPMG’s behalf, the FY21 Audit report on 7 December 2021.
3.3. As noted above, Carr’s shares are listed on the main market of the London Stock
Exchange and throughout FY21 Carr’s was a PIE as defined in Regulation 2 of the
Statutory Auditors and Third Country Auditors Regulations 2016 (“SATCAR”). At the end
of FY21 Carr’s had a market capitalisation of c.£147.8m.
3.4. Carr’s described its corporate group in its Annual Report for FY21 as “an international
group investing in the agricultural and engineering sectors”. It stated that “Carr’s Group
plc is an international leader in manufacturing and supplying value-adding products and
solutions, with market leading brands and robust market positions in Agriculture and
Engineering. We supply customers in over 50 countries around the world.” It reported
its financial performance under the headings of three divisions: Speciality Agriculture,
Agricultural Supplies and Engineering. The reported revenue for these divisions was
£68.5m, £297.5m and £51.3m respectively. Carr’s reported employing 1,149 people at
the end of FY21.
3.5. Carr’s investments in FY21 included a stake in CBAO. According to Carr’s Annual
Report for FY21, Carr’s owned 49% of CBAO’s issued share capital and held 33% of its
board representation. CBAO was accounted for as an associate in Carr’s FY21 financial
statements and accordingly, CBAO’s financial results were incorporated into Carr’s
FY21 financial statements.
3.6. CBAO’s financial statements for FY21 described its operations as the manufacture and
supply of compound animal feed. Its reported revenue in those statements was £138m
(of which £137m was generated from sales to the Carr’s Group). As an associate of
Carr’s, the financial results of CBAO were included in a single line, Share of post-tax
results of associate, totalling £831k, within the Carr’s consolidated income statement.

5 FRC Key Facts and Trends in the Accountancy Profession, August 2022
(https://media.frc.org.uk/documents/FRC_Key_Facts_and_Trends_in_the_Accountancy_Profession_
August_2022.pdf)

8
OFFICIAL
3.7. In FY21 CBAO was audited by Firm X, who had audited CBAO continuously from the
year ended 31 August 2002. Firm X Partner had performed the role of Senior Statutory
Auditor for CBAO’s audit since the year ended 4 September 2016. Accordingly, FY21
was Firm X Partner’s sixth year as the Senior Statutory Auditor for CBAO.
Audit planning in FY21

3.8. KPMG’s planning for the FY21 Audit included steps in relation to CBAO and Firm X. On
27 May 2021 representatives of KPMG met Firm X Partner and others from Firm X for a
planning meeting in relation to the FY21 Audit of CBAO. The Agenda for this meeting
included “Logistics”, with an agenda item of “roles and responsibilities (including Partner
rotation policies)”. KPMG recorded next to this item “no issues noted”.
3.9. KPMG’s obligations in relation to Firm X included identifying and avoiding threats to its
independence. In an internal KPMG spreadsheet called “Carr’s Review Note Summary”,
dated 26 July 2021, Mr Plumb had created a “Review Note” stating “is there anything
we need to do to assess [the] independence of [Firm X]”. No further entries were added
to this note and the evidence does not explain whether or how Mr Plumb’s query was
resolved.
3.10. Other internal KPMG spreadsheets showed the scoping of components such as CBAO
for the purpose of the FY21 Audit. KPMG’s Excel spreadsheet that formed its scoping
workpaper for FY21 planning showed that KPMG used three metrics to identify a
component as “financially significant”: revenue, Profit before Tax from Continuing
Operations (“PBTCO”), and total assets. CBAO is shown as a “significant component”
in that workpaper due to it being forecast to contribute over 5% of the Group’s PBTCO.
The spreadsheet, titled “2.8.1.3.0010 Carrs Group 2021 Scoping WP”, thus showed
CBAO as a “financially significant component”. KPMG later described this scoping in an
internal email of 4 December 2022 as follows:
““when the instructions were issued this component was borderline on financial
significance (forecast 5.5% PBT vs 5% threshold) so we included it as a financially
significant component (hence the classification in A.01). It was at final scoping
when the calculations indicated it was below the financial significance (3.5% v 5%)
threshold”.
3.11. Notwithstanding these revised calculations, CBAO remained scoped by the audit team
as a financially significant component. A total of nine components of Carr’s were

9
OFFICIAL
designated for “full scope” consideration by the Carr’s FY21 Audit team.6 Of these,
CBAO was the only one audited by a firm outside of KPMG’s network.
3.12. CBAO was the principal employer of a defined benefit pension scheme in surplus. Carr’s
was exposed to a Group-level significant audit risk arising from the valuation of its share
of what KPMG described in its relevant workpaper as the CBAO net defined benefit
pension scheme surplus. This posed complex calculation issues.
3.13. This “2.8.1.3.0010 Carrs Group 2021 Scoping WP” spreadsheet listed the component
auditors of the Group and stated that “Any requirements for the use of Component
Auditors will be considered in line with ISA 600”.
3.14. On 8 June 2021 KPMG presented its audit plan and strategy report for the FY21 Audit
to Carr’s Audit committee. Its presentation for that meeting identified CBAO as
“financially significant” and “exposed to group level significant risks”. CBAO’s auditor
was shown as Firm X, albeit the auditing of the relevant pension scheme would be done
by KPMG, such that no group significant risks were audited by Firm X. The presentation
stated that because Carr’s was a PIE, when KPMG engaged with the component auditor
for CBAO they would “…seek appropriate confirmation of their independence in line with
ethical standards”.
Information gathering and independence considerations by the Respondents
3.15. In January 2021 KPMG wrote to Firm X advising them of changes arising from the 2019
Ethical Standard and how this would impact upon their Group audit instructions for the
FY21 Audit. In this communication, the KPMG audit team made it clear that non-KPMG-
network audit firms involved in a group audit (such as Firm X) would be required to follow
the requirements of the 2019 Ethical Standard (as opposed to the IESBA Code7 which
had previously applied). It remained the Respondents’ obligation not to rely on Firm X’s
work during the FY21 Audit, unless the requirements of the 2019 Ethical Standard had
been met.

6 The Carr’s Group included a total of 30 components in FY21, which were categorised by the Carr’s
FY21 Audit Team between “Full scope”, “Specified AP” and “Residual”. The categorisation was based
on a risk assessment and determined the volume and nature of audit work to be performed by KPMG.
“Full scope” audits required the most audit work and “Residual” the least. All “Full scope” components
were designated as “financially significant” and none of the remainder were designated as such.

7 I.e. the prevailing International Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants issued by the
International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants.

10
OFFICIAL
3.16. On 7 September 2021 KPMG sent Firm X a Group Audit Instructions document (“GAI”)
seeking information on a number of matters relevant to the FY21 Audit. In error, the
version of the GAI which KPMG sent Firm X had been superseded as it did not take
account of the requirements of the 2019 Ethical Standard (which had become effective
on 15 March 2020).8 The GAI did not therefore refer to the requirement for a KAP to
cease their involvement in a Statutory Audit after five years, nor refer to the “non-audit
services” that were prohibited by the 2019 Ethical Standard for significant affiliates of
listed entities. CBAO was such an affiliate.
3.17. The GAI also identified, in its appendices, that CBAO had been classified by KPMG as
“individually financially significant”.
3.18. ISA 600 applied to the FY21 Audit and required the Carr’s FY21 Audit team to evaluate
and review the work performed by the component auditor. As such, the GAI required
Firm X to send back to KPMG several forms in which they were required either to confirm
compliance with ethics and independence requirements or give reasons as to why such
confirmations could not be made. Firm X provided responsive information by way of
those forms in September 2021. These responses were considered by the KPMG audit
team, Mr Plumb and KPMG’s Engagement Quality Control Reviewer for the FY21 Audit
(“EQCR”) before being signed off by Mr Plumb. The responses identified, among other
things, that:
3.18.1. That Firm X understood and would comply with “the ethical requirements,
including independence requirements, described in the FRC Ethical Standard
that are relevant to the audit of the Group financial statements.” This response
did not, however, refer specifically to the 2019 Ethical Standard;
3.18.2. A familiarity threat to Firm X’s independence was mitigated by the appointment
of an EQCR; and
3.18.3. Firm X was also providing to CBAO certain non-audit services (“NAS”),
comprising the preparation of accounts from trial balances and the preparation
of tax computations: “With regards to the provision of non audit services, [Firm
X] are engaged to prepare the statutory accounts of the component as well as
the corporation taxation computation. Both of these are completed from the
information and records provided by the client. Any matters of judgement or
decision making, if relevant, are taken by the components informed

8 2019 Ethical Standard paragraph 1.69.

11
OFFICIAL
management and documented as such. The corporation tax computation is
prepared and reviewed by [Firm X’s] corporate tax team which are completely
independent to the audit team”.
3.19. Firm X’s audit workpapers showed that in each of FY19, FY20 and FY21, they:
3.19.1. noted that a familiarity threat arose from their long association with the CBAO
audit, and, that “the client was satisfied that [Firm X Partner] [was] sufficiently
independent and objective to continue his involvement in the audit”, which
obviated the need for safeguards; and
3.19.2. considered the possibility of a management threat and a self-review threat
arising from the provision of the aforementioned NAS, and implemented
safeguards.
3.20. No allegations or findings are made in this Final Settlement Decision Notice against Firm
X in respect of their consideration of such threats, or their audit work generally.
3.21. In October 2021, KPMG’s Head of Ethics and Independence emailed all KPMG audit
partners of PIEs to require that partner rotation data should be checked for accuracy
and completeness, and specific confirmation provided that such checks had been made.
At Mr Plumb’s request, the audit team considered the auditor rotation data for Carr’s,
alongside a member of the KPMG second line of defence (“2LD”) team. It was confirmed
to Mr Plumb that the data held for the FY21 Audit was accurate, but no comment was
made on the completeness of the data.
3.22. On 1 November 2021 the KPMG audit team attended a clearance meeting with Firm X
and a Director of CBAO to discuss Firm X’s audit of CBAO. No significant issues were
raised in respect of the audit generally, including any relating to independence issues.
A review of the Firm X audit file by the KPMG group audit team took place (remotely by
way of a video call) on 9 November 2021.
3.23. On 10 November 2021 Firm X provided Mr Plumb with a Completion Memo form. This
included a question covering “issues with independence and ethical requirements,
including any team rotation requirements”. Firm X answered: “nothing to report”.
3.24. A report by Firm X to CBAO’s directors in November 20219 identified that Firm X’s audit
team had had a “long term association” with the CBAO audit. This document was

9 The copy of the document on the KPMG audit file is dated “XX November 2021”.

12
OFFICIAL
provided to KPMG in the course of the FY21 Audit and reviewed by the KPMG audit
team, Mr Plumb and the EQCR.
3.25. KPMG maintained a 2LD observation tracker spreadsheet for the FY21 Audit, containing
comments exchanged between the reviewer and members of the audit team. This
included:
3.25.1. Identification of CBAO as an “ISA 600 component”;
3.25.2. A reference to versions of the GAI having been updated, and a query that the
version of the GAI used by the audit team did not appear tailored to the fact that
Firm X was not a KPMG member firm;
3.25.3. An entry that it “would be good to document whether the senior team members
eg the RI / manager etc have changed from [Firm X] or if there is consistency
[Year on Year]. Also what their qualifications are as individuals”; and
3.25.4. A query from the reviewer as to whether the Partner Rotation Table that KPMG
used on the audit file included all relevant individuals. This did not prompt the
audit team to notice that personnel from Firm X were not included on that
Partner Rotation Table.
3.26. In total, the 2LD reviewer raised five questions relating to component audit partner
rotation, the identification of component audit partners as KAPs, the roles and tenure of
Firm X’s audit team members, and changes in the GAI appendices for components. The
2LD observation tracker spreadsheet was shared with the audit team, including Mr
Plumb, the KPMG EQCR and a senior member of the audit team, but not appropriately
addressed by the Respondents.
3.27. None of KPMG’s FY21 Audit workpapers addressed whether CBAO was a “material
subsidiary”, which was a prerequisite for the appropriate consideration of whether the
Firm X Partner was a KAP for the purposes of paragraph 3.10 of the 2019 Ethical
Standard. Nor do the workpapers address his length of tenure as Statutory Auditor for
CBAO.
3.28. Notwithstanding the matters identified above:
3.28.1. The KPMG audit team members failed to appreciate the significance of the
familiarity threat or the “long term association” of Firm X with the CBAO audit.
As a result of this failure, no further enquiries were made of Firm X in relation
to the KAP’s tenure; nor was any assessment undertaken as to whether the
KAP’s continued participation in the CBAO audit was permitted in FY21.

13
OFFICIAL
3.28.2. None of the KPMG audit team members identified that NAS were provided to
CBAO by Firm X. As a result of the Respondents’ failure to identify the provision
of the NAS, no further enquiries were made of Firm X as to the nature of the
services and nor was there an assessment as to the permissibility of the
services and / or any associated threats or safeguards.
Audit team conclusions in relation to independence of component auditors

3.29. KPMG completed, among other things, an ISA UK 600 workpaper headed “Involvement
in significant components”. This stated that it was to be reviewed by Mr Plumb. It
included an entry that KPMG had requested written confirmation from the component
auditor that they meet applicable independence and ethical requirements, and showed
that KPMG considered Firm X did meet those requirements.
3.30. On 16 November 2021 KPMG made a presentation to Carr’s Audit Committee which
included information about KPMG’s involvement with component auditors. The
presentation described a senior member of KPMG’s audit team reviewing the files of
Firm X, and referred to Firm X, Mr Plumb and a senior member of KPMG’s audit team
participating in planning and clearance meetings. The presentation slides then
confirmed the audit independence of KPMG, and its compliance with the ethical
requirements of the 2019 Ethical Standard, without reference to the position of Firm X.
3.31. On 3 December 2021 KPMG made a further presentation to the Audit Committee of
Carr’s, including stating that “our ISA 600 reviews of [another component]10 and CBAO
files are also now substantially complete”.
3.32. On 7 December 2021 Mr Plumb signed the audit report for the FY21 Audit, in which he
stated on behalf of KPMG, “We have fulfilled our ethical responsibilities under, and we
remain independent of, the Group in accordance with UK ethical requirements including
the FRC Ethical Standard as applied to listed public interest entities”. This report
included references to KPMG instructing component auditors as to the significant areas
for them to cover, and to meetings being held with those component auditors “to assess
the audit risks and strategy”.
3.33. Mr Plumb and the rest of the audit team raised no issues in connection with the FY21
Audit report, or at all, concerning (i) Firm X’s compliance with the 2019 Ethical Standard

10 Another component of Carr’s which was audited by a KPMG network firm in Germany. Name
anonymised.

14
OFFICIAL
or (ii) the steps taken and not taken by KPMG to satisfy itself as to the independence of
Firm X, before using the work of that firm as a component auditor.
3.34. KPMG invoiced Carr’s £523,427 (including outlays and overruns) for audit services on
the FY21 Audit. Firm X’s audit fee for the audit of CBAO was £17,500.
Discovery and acceptance of breaches
3.35. On 7 February 2022 KPMG resigned as the auditors of Carr’s following a tender
exercise. They were replaced by a firm referred to herein as “Firm Y”, for the financial
period ended 3 September 2022 (“FY22”) onwards. During the audit of Carr’s financial
statements for FY22, Firm Y identified concerns regarding compliance with the 2019
Ethical Standard: (i) Firm X Partner, being a KAP, had performed the role of Statutory
Auditor for more than five years; and (ii) Firm X had provided certain tax and accounting
services to CBAO, which were prohibited for significant affiliates pursuant to the 2019
Ethical Standard (paragraphs 5.71 and 5.120(a)).
3.36. Firm Y reached the conclusion that they were not permitted by the 2019 Ethical Standard
to place reliance on the audit work conducted by Firm X in respect of CBAO. On 22
November 2022, Carr’s announced a delay to the publication of Carr’s FY22 financial
statements. The Audit Committee report to the FY22 financial statements explained in
this regard:
“Issues identified during the audit relating to the independence of the auditor of
the Group’s associate company contributed to a delay in the finalisation of the

Category 1 – Breaches by the Respondents in relation to KAP rotation requirements
The Respondents failed to ensure that the requirements of paragraph 3.10 of the 2019
Ethical Standard were complied with during the FY21 Audit. The Respondents
consequently breached paragraph 1.47 (in conjunction with A2.4) of the 2019 Ethical
Standard and paragraphs 11 and 19(a) of ISA (UK) 600 in relation to the participation of
the Firm X Partner in the FY21 Statutory Audit of CBAO.
5.1. As noted in Section 2 above, the Respondents’ obligations under the 2019 Ethical
Standard included an obligation regarding other firms, under paragraph 1.47 of the 2019
Ethical Standard. This provides:
“In order to use the work of another firm (including network firms) for the purpose
of an engagement, the lead firm for the engagement has to obtain sufficient
appropriate evidence and be satisfied that such another firm is independent of
each entity relevant to the engagement in accordance with supporting ethical
provision 2.4 of this Ethical Standard”.
5.2. The supporting ethical provision A2.4 further required that:
“For each engagement, the firm and the engagement partner (in the case of the
engagement partner insofar as they are able to do so) shall ensure that the firm’s
independence is not compromised as a result of conditions or relationships that
would compromise the independence of a network firm (whether or not its work is
used in the conduct of the engagement) or an other firm whose work is used in the
conduct of the engagement, having regard to the ethical requirements in this
Ethical Standard that are relevant to the engagement.”
5.3. Under ISA (UK) 600 paragraph 19(a), the Respondents were obliged to obtain an
understanding of whether Firm X understood and would comply with relevant ethical
requirements and was independent:
“If the group engagement team plans to request a component auditor to perform
work on the financial information of a component, the group engagement team
shall obtain an understanding of the following: (Ref: Para. A32–A35) (a) Whether
the component auditor understands and will comply with the ethical requirements
that are relevant to the group audit and, in particular, is independent. (Ref: Para.
A37–A37-1)”
5.4. The definition of “group engagement team” at paragraph 9 of ISA (UK) 600 includes Mr
Plumb as the group engagement partner.

engagement team: (i) That is of individual financial significance to the group, or
(ii) That, due to its specific nature or circumstances, is likely to include
significant risks of material misstatement of the group financial statements.”
5.13.3. CBAO was assessed by KPMG as a financially significant component of Carr’s
due to its forecast contribution of over 5% of the Group’s PBTCO, and this

5.13.5. Firm X provided services to CBAO in FY21 that included the preparation of
current tax calculations in the form of corporation tax computations, which might
reasonably have been expected to be used by CBAO when preparing

SANCTIONS
6.1. Paragraph 10 of the FRC’s Sanctions Policy (Audit Enforcement Procedure) (the
“Policy”) provides that Sanctions are intended to be effective, proportionate and
dissuasive. The reasons for imposing Sanctions are identified in paragraph 11 of the
Policy as the following:
6.1.1.
to declare and uphold proper standards of conduct amongst Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms and to maintain and enhance the quality and reliability
of future audits;
6.1.2.
to maintain and promote public and market confidence in Statutory Auditors
and Statutory Audit Firms and the quality of their audits and in the regulation of
the accountancy profession;
6.1.3.
to protect the public from Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms whose
conduct has fallen short of the Relevant Requirements; and
6.1.4.
to deter Statutory Auditors and Statutory Audit Firms from breaching the
Relevant Requirements relating to Statutory Audit.
6.2. In considering the Sanctions to be imposed, Executive Counsel has, in summary,
considered the following matters in accordance with the Policy.

Nature, extent and importance of the Relevant Requirements
6.3. It is of fundamental importance that Statutory Auditors comply with the ethical standards
applicable to their work. As explained in paragraphs I1 to I4 of the 2019 Ethical Standard:
[I1] “A fundamental objective of any [audit or other public interest assurance]
engagement is that the intended users trust and have confidence that the audit or
assurance opinion is professionally sound and objective. This should enhance the

23
OFFICIAL
credibility for users of the information the opinion covers (e.g. in the case of an
audit engagement, the financial statements)…”
[I3] “… principal-agent relationships (where the users are the principals and the
directors and auditors of the entity their agents) give rise to the potential for
conflicts of interests that need to be addressed if the user is to have trust and
confidence in the audit/assurance process, the subject matter information and the
directors of the entity itself…”
[I4] “In the context of an engagement, such conflicts of interest create a potential
risk (threat) that the practitioner’s judgment or actions in conducting or determining
the outcome of the engagement may be unduly influenced by interests other than
those of the intended user… if the practitioner is unduly influenced by them, this
may prejudice the interests of the intended users, which should be paramount.”
6.4. The 2019 Ethical Standard establishes a framework of ethical outcomes that are
required to be met by the auditor, to provide a basis for user trust and confidence in the
integrity and objectivity of the practitioner in performing the engagement14.
6.5. The 2019 Ethical Standard defines the principle of Independence in the following
manner15:
“In relation to each engagement, the firm, and each covered person, shall
ensure…that the firm and each covered person is free from conditions and
relationships which would make it probable that an objective, reasonable and
informed third party would conclude the independence of the firm or any covered
person is compromised.”
6.6. Threats to Independence can arise by, among other things:
6.6.1. the participation in the audit of partners or staff in senior positions for long periods,
including by way of self-review or familiarity threats; or
6.6.2. the provision of NAS, including by way of self-interest threat, management threat,
advocacy threat and self-review threat.

6.7.2. The provision of certain NAS.

6.31. KPMG implemented the remedial measures summarised at paragraph 6.21 above.
